```{r} #| label: full_code_display #| eval: true #| echo: false #| warning: false #| message: false #| out-height: '60%' #| out-width: '60%' #| fig-align: right library(ggplot2) library(dplyr) set.seed(1985) oregon_trail <- tibble( party_id = 1:300, profession = rep(c("Banker", "Carpenter", "Farmer"), each = 100)) |> mutate(profession = factor(profession, levels = c("Banker", "Carpenter", "Farmer")), median_days = c(Banker = 140, Carpenter = 155, Farmer = 170)[as.character(profession)], days_to_oregon = round(rlnorm(n(), meanlog = log(median_days), sdlog = 0.2))) |> select(party_id, profession, days_to_oregon) labs_grp_boxplots <- labs( title = "The Oregon Trail", caption = "Simulated data", subtitle = "Days for 100 parties of each profession to reach Oregon", x = "Profession", fill = "Profession", y = "Days to reach Oregon") ggp2_grp_boxplots <- ggplot(data = oregon_trail, aes(x = profession, y = days_to_oregon, fill = profession)) + geom_boxplot(alpha = 2/3, show.legend = FALSE) ggp2_grp_boxplots + labs_grp_boxplots ``` ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #02577A;"} **Requirements:** ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; color: #282b2d;"} **✅ a categorical variable** ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; color: #282b2d;"} **✅ a numeric (continuous) variable** ::: :::: ## Description Grouped box plots display five different statistical measures across a series of categories, or groups, of a discrete, ordinal, or interval variable. The five statistical measures are 1) the first quartile, 2) the second quartile, and 3) the third quartile. The fourth and fifth values are the largest/smallest values no further than 1.5 X inter-quartile range from the hinges. ## Set up ::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"} **PACKAGES:** ::: Install packages. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ```{r} #| label: pkg_code_grp_boxplots #| code-fold: show #| eval: false #| echo: true #| warning: false #| message: false #| results: hide library(ggplot2) library(dplyr) # for tibble() and data manipulation ``` ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"} **DATA:** ::: In *The Oregon Trail*, you picked a profession before you set out, and it decided how much money (and how many supplies) your party started with. We'll simulate how many days it took 100 parties of each profession to reach Oregon. Each profession gets its own typical trip length (`median_days`), and `rlnorm()` draws each trip from a log normal distribution, so a few unlucky parties (dysentery, broken axles, lost oxen) take much longer than the rest. Setting the seed with `set.seed()` means you'll get the same 300 trips every time you run the code below. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ```{r} #| label: data_code_grp_boxplots #| code-fold: show #| eval: true #| echo: true set.seed(1985) oregon_trail <- tibble( party_id = 1:300, profession = rep(c("Banker", "Carpenter", "Farmer"), each = 100)) |> mutate(profession = factor(profession, levels = c("Banker", "Carpenter", "Farmer")), median_days = c(Banker = 140, Carpenter = 155, Farmer = 170)[as.character(profession)], days_to_oregon = round(rlnorm(n(), meanlog = log(median_days), sdlog = 0.2))) |> select(party_id, profession, days_to_oregon) glimpse(oregon_trail) ``` ::: ## Distribution Grouped box plots compare five summary numbers across groups. When the data are skewed, those five numbers aren't evenly spaced: the median sits closer to the bottom of the box, and the upper whisker is longer than the lower one. Below we'll move from the trips, to a picture, to the formula. ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **COUNT IT:** ::: Start with the first eight trips (all bankers). ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ```{r} #| label: count_values_grp_boxplots #| code-fold: show #| eval: true #| echo: true head(oregon_trail$days_to_oregon, 8) ``` ::: These trips took between 112 and 180 days. The summary below shows each profession's quartiles. For every profession, the distance from the median up to the third quartile (`upper_gap`) is larger than the distance down to the first quartile (`lower_gap`). ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ```{r} #| label: count_summary_grp_boxplots #| code-fold: show #| eval: true #| echo: true oregon_trail |> group_by(profession) |> summarise(q1 = quantile(days_to_oregon, 0.25), median = median(days_to_oregon), q3 = quantile(days_to_oregon, 0.75)) |> mutate(lower_gap = median - q1, upper_gap = q3 - median) ``` ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **DRAW IT:** ::: The box plots on the left use days, so each box is lopsided: the median line sits low in the box, and the long trips stretch the upper whiskers (the farmers even have a few outliers). The box plots on the right put the same trips on a log scale with `scale_y_log10()`. On the log scale the boxes are symmetric and the whiskers are about the same length on both sides. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ```{r} #| label: draw_grp_boxplots #| code-fold: show #| eval: true #| echo: true #| layout-ncol: 2 ggplot(oregon_trail, aes(x = profession, y = days_to_oregon, fill = profession)) + geom_boxplot(alpha = 2/3, show.legend = FALSE) + labs(title = "Days", x = NULL, y = "Days to reach Oregon") ggplot(oregon_trail, aes(x = profession, y = days_to_oregon, fill = profession)) + geom_boxplot(alpha = 2/3, show.legend = FALSE) + scale_y_log10() + labs(title = "Log scale", x = NULL, y = "Days (log scale)") ``` ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **NAME IT:** ::: Each profession's trips come from a [log normal distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Log-normal_distribution), the same distribution as the Beanie Babies prices in the violin plot chapter: $$ \log(X_{\text{profession}}) \sim \text{Normal}(\log(m_{\text{profession}}), \; \sigma = 0.2), \quad m = (140, 155, 170) $$ On the log scale, the quartiles sit $0.674\,\sigma$ above and below the center, which is why the log scale boxes are symmetric. Back on the day scale, those quartiles become $m\,e^{-0.674 \times 0.2}$ and $m\,e^{0.674 \times 0.2}$: for bankers, about 122 and 160 days. That's 18 days below the median but 20 days above it, and the gap grows the further out you go, which is why the upper whiskers are longer. Try a larger `sdlog` in `rlnorm()` and the boxes become even more lopsided. ## Grammar ::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"} **CODE:** ::: - Create labels with `labs()` - Initialize the graph with `ggplot()` and provide `data` - Map `profession` to the `x` axis and to `fill` - Map `days_to_oregon` to the `y` axis - Add `geom_boxplot()` and set the `alpha` to `2/3` - Remove the legend with `show.legend = FALSE` ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ```{r} #| label: code_graph_grp_boxplots #| code-fold: show #| eval: false #| echo: true #| warning: false #| message: false #| out-height: '100%' #| out-width: '100%' labs_grp_boxplots <- labs( title = "The Oregon Trail", caption = "Simulated data", subtitle = "Days for 100 parties of each profession to reach Oregon", x = "Profession", fill = "Profession", y = "Days to reach Oregon") ggp2_grp_boxplots <- ggplot(data = oregon_trail, aes(x = profession, y = days_to_oregon, fill = profession)) + geom_boxplot(alpha = 2/3, show.legend = FALSE) ggp2_grp_boxplots + labs_grp_boxplots ``` ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"} **GRAPH:** ::: When a categorical variable is supplied, the plot will contain a box for each level or group. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ```{r} #| label: create_graph_grp_boxplots #| eval: true #| echo: false #| warning: false #| message: false #| out-height: '100%' #| out-width: '100%' #| layout-nrow: 1 labs_grp_boxplots <- labs( title = "The Oregon Trail", caption = "Simulated data", subtitle = "Days for 100 parties of each profession to reach Oregon", x = "Profession", fill = "Profession", y = "Days to reach Oregon") ggp2_grp_boxplots <- ggplot(data = oregon_trail, aes(x = profession, y = days_to_oregon, fill = profession)) + geom_boxplot(alpha = 2/3, show.legend = FALSE) ggp2_grp_boxplots + labs_grp_boxplots ``` ::: ## More info ### Notches Add notches to the box plot using the `notch = TRUE` and `notchwidth` arguments. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ```{r} #| label: notches_boxplots #| eval: true #| echo: true #| warning: false #| message: false #| out-height: '100%' #| out-width: '100%' #| layout-nrow: 1 ggp2_grp_box_notch <- ggplot(data = oregon_trail, aes(x = profession, y = days_to_oregon, fill = profession)) + geom_boxplot( notch = TRUE, notchwidth = 0.85, alpha = 2/3, show.legend = FALSE) ggp2_grp_box_notch + labs_grp_boxplots ``` ::: ### Outliers Box plots display outliers using points, and we can change the color these using the `outlier.colour` argument. Inside the `geom_boxplot()`, we map `profession` to `color` and set `outlier.colour` to `NULL`: ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ```{r} #| label: outliers_boxplots #| eval: true #| echo: true #| warning: false #| message: false #| out-height: '100%' #| out-width: '100%' #| layout-nrow: 1 ggp2_grp_box_outliers <- ggplot(data = oregon_trail, aes(x = profession, y = days_to_oregon, fill = profession)) + geom_boxplot(aes(color = profession), outlier.colour = NULL, outlier.size = 2, notch = TRUE, notchwidth = 0.85, alpha = 2/3, show.legend = FALSE) ggp2_grp_box_outliers + labs_grp_boxplots ``` :::
